doc.title: Jerry Hey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 2, 2023

title: Quincy Jones, David Foster, Maurice White and George Duke as producers
summary: Hey compares the producers: Quincy's personality, Foster's brilliance in the studio, Maurice White's sung parts, and George Duke.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: What makes Quincy Jones and David Foster and those tremendously successful producers, is there a similarity to their personalities or what made them so successful?

Quincy is all about personality. You just, when you go into the studio with him you feel like the record would fail if you weren’t in on this session. That’s how he makes you feel, that you are a major part of this record-making process. And it’s family, it’s — you have a good time, you play great music, great engineer, great songs. He always works with the best artists. You know how can it not be great? That’s Quincy’s thing. I mean plus he picks songs you know. He always says the song comes first and yes it does. And anything else doesn’t really matter if you’ve got a great song. David Foster is a brilliant musician, and like I said he can sit down and play anything right away. There was a Jarreau session © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

that he was playing on with Abraham Laboriel, bass; Lukather on guitar; I believe it was Steve Gadd on drums; and Jay Graydon, the producer/guitar player also, didn’t like the bridge. So Jay said, “David, I don’t really like the bridge you know, let’s work on the bridge.” So with they’re all — including me — standing around the piano with David Foster and he goes [scats] how’s that? And it was like, wow that was ridiculous. I mean this was just like cold doing this. And David goes, “Na, try something else.” And David would go [scats] how’s that? Totally different, equally as amazing. He did six or seven like that, just like eight-bar changes that were like guys would kill for any of those eight bars. Brilliant. And you know he just is, he’s fantastic in the studio, just amazing, totally different approach personality wise than Quincy. Quincy makes you feel like, you know, the world revolves around you, and David it’s all about David as the producer, you know regardless of who you are, even if you’re Celine Dion or Whitney Houston or anything, it’s David is in charge there. But you know some of the best things I’ve ever done are with David. You know it’s always, the music is always great. Jay Graydon is another musician coming along with David, a little less hands-on than David. David is really hands-on. Maurice White, another brilliant producer with Earth, Wind & Fire — you know I learned some things with Maurice White that would — as I was saying before when we would do horn parts and he would sing a part. And I’d say, “Well you know Maurice that note’s really, it’s not really in the chord there that you’re singing.” He said, “I think it’s going to work.” And okay, you go out and you play it and you kind of force it into the, okay I get it, and then the more you listen to it’s like yeah, I like it.
And I wouldn’t have thought of that, right.

Yeah no, no way. So you know each producer that I’ve worked with has a little bit different approach as to how they get to finished product. You know George Duke, great guy, great player, you know just kind of knows the whole thing. He let me do some arranging for him.
